body:
Marissa Cole: We need to lock what the *customer-visible* model changelog includes vs what stays internal. This keeps coming up in the PRD + support threads. I want a clear rule we can hand to Eng + Docs.

Marissa Cole: Proposal: customer sees (1) what changed, (2) whether they should do anything, (3) compatibility/constraints, (4) timelines (deprecation), and (5) where to learn more (links). Internal notes (ops/debug/vendor stuff) stays internal-only.

Paula Mendes: +1. Rollouts angle: if a customer is running a canary/A-B and sees drift, they need a way to answer “did the model change?” without opening a support ticket.

Quentin Harris: For the schema we already have fields that are clearly internal (kernel config, capacity tier routing notes, vendor provenance details). But the tricky part is perf deltas + eval links.

Elliot Price: Docs POV: we need a consistent template and a do/don’t list. We can’t ship release notes that read like internal Jira comments.

Wei Chen: Agree. Also, if we include numbers, we’ll get “why did I not see that improvement?” questions forever bc workloads differ.

Dylan Brooks: From Eng: perf deltas are tempting because they’re objective-ish, but they’re also the highest-risk for misinterpretation. Also there’s the issue of “perf delta relative to what baseline?” and whether it’s on hosted vs dedicated vs private.

Dev Patel: Support angle: customers ask two things: (a) “did behavior change?” (quality/safety) and (b) “did latency/cost change?” If we don’t give anything, they assume we’re hiding it. If we give hard numbers, they’ll hold us to them.

Marissa Cole: Right, so maybe we include *directional* perf info + caveats. Like “Improved throughput for long-context workloads” vs “+18% tok/s”.

Paula Mendes: But enterprise procurement teams sometimes explicitly ask for “performance regressions” to be called out. Not necessarily exact numbers, but some acknowledgement.

Jada Williams: Workflow thought: we can make “Performance notes” a required section, but allow either:
- “No material performance changes expected.”
- “Performance changes expected for X scenario.”
And only optionally include metrics if there’s a published benchmark.

Tessa Morgan: UX: if we include a “Performance” section, it can be collapsed by default on the model version page, with a tooltip explaining variability.

Quentin Harris: Another angle: we *can* include numbers but tie them to a specific standardized benchmark + environment, e.g. “Redwood Bench v2026-02 on A100 80GB, seq=8k, batch=…”. That’s honest but still a lot.

Wei Chen: That’s the kind of detail we usually don’t want in a customer-facing note. It becomes a wall of text.

Elliot Price: Also, it forces docs to keep a public “benchmark spec” page up to date. If we do it, we need to commit to maintaining it.

Dylan Brooks: There’s also the “this change is due to runtime/kernel update not model weights” problem. If we attribute perf deltas in model changelog, we’re mixing concerns.

Marissa Cole: For v1, I’d rather keep perf deltas high level and cross-link to runtime release notes when it’s runtime-driven.

Dev Patel: +1. Support can use a short statement + link rather than customers screenshotting a % and asking why they got -3%.

Paula Mendes: What about eval links? If we don’t include any quality proof, customers will ask “how do you know it’s better?”

Quentin Harris: We have internal eval dashboards with prompt sets and metrics. Those dashboards include some internal-only datasets and account names. We can’t link that directly.

Wei Chen: Could we link to a sanitized “Model Quality” page that only shows public eval sets / generalized metrics?

Elliot Price: We can, but v1 scope says no auto narratives from eval diffs. Linking is okay if it’s stable and customer-safe.

Dylan Brooks: Engineering can generate a stable URL per model_version to a public-ish eval summary, but we’d need an allowlist of what metrics/datasets are safe.

Marissa Cole: Here’s a concrete policy draft:
1) Customer-facing changelog MUST NOT include: internal model nicknames, vendor contract details, infrastructure topology, kernel names, raw incident references, internal dashboards.
2) Customer-facing changelog SHOULD include: 
- Summary (1–3 bullets)
- Impact (who is affected)
- Compatibility (context length, tool/function calling support, structured output caveats)
- Deprecation timelines + replacement
- Links: docs page + (optional) eval summary link if customer-safe
3) Performance section:
- Default: qualitative statement only.
- Numeric deltas only if they are backed by a public benchmark page with explicit environment + variance disclaimer, and *only* for “material” changes.

Paula Mendes: I like that. Can we define “material” for numeric? Otherwise we’ll argue every time.

Jada Williams: Suggest: material = 
- latency p50/p95 change >10% on Redwood standard benchmark OR
- cost per 1k tokens change >10% OR
- explicit known regression.

Dev Patel: Please include “known regression” even if <10%. If we *know* something is worse for a segment, we should say it.

Wei Chen: Re eval links: we can phrase as “Evaluation summary” and keep it optional. Also make sure it doesn’t look like we’re guaranteeing quality.

Elliot Price: Wording idea: “See evaluation summary (Redwood-curated benchmarks). Results may vary by prompt distribution and settings.”

Quentin Harris: If we do eval links, we need to ensure the generator can’t accidentally include internal-only link targets. This probably needs a hard-coded host allowlist.

Dylan Brooks: +1, plus we should make the generator treat eval links as a separate field validated server-side.

Tessa Morgan: UI: If no eval link exists, don’t show an empty “Evaluation” section. If it exists, show it as “Learn more” not “Proof.”

Marissa Cole: Ok, decision for v1 (unless strong objections):
- No raw perf deltas by default.
- Allow numeric deltas only when backed by a published benchmark spec page + material threshold.
- Eval links allowed only to a customer-safe eval summary page (not internal dashboards), optional per entry.
- Everything else internal goes in internal_notes, never published.

Paula Mendes: Works for me. We should capture this in the style guide + schema allowlist.

Elliot Price: I’ll update the docs style guide with these rules + examples of acceptable phrasing.

Wei Chen: Same. I can draft a “good vs bad” section (e.g., “improved long-context stability” vs “switched to kernel XYZ”).

Dev Patel: Can we add one more: “Support readiness” internal-only checklist / links. That content shouldn’t leak but should be easy for Support to find.

Marissa Cole: Yes — internal_notes can include support readiness links and known issues, but customers get a sanitized “Known issues” section only if we’re comfortable publishing it.

Quentin Harris: We should make “Known issues” optional but strongly recommended when there is any behavior change, with a customer-safe workaround if possible.

Dylan Brooks: +1. Also call out that “no known issues” is allowed so it doesn’t look like we forgot.

Jada Williams: I’ll take an action item to encode this into the workflow states (draft/in_review/published) with a checklist item: “No internal-only content” + “Perf section meets policy.”

Marissa Cole: Great. I’m linking this thread in PM-801. We’ll formalize in the PRD + style guide.

Linear (bot): Marissa Cole linked this thread to PM-801: “Define customer-facing release note taxonomy (bugfix vs perf vs compatibility vs deprecation) and required sections per change type.”

Elliot Price: Also: we should explicitly say “don’t include absolute latency numbers.” Customers will ask “is this your infra or mine?” So we stick to relative/per-scenario.

Wei Chen: :thumbsup: and we can add a sentence in the template: “Performance can vary by deployment mode (Hosted/Dedicated/Private) and request mix.”

Paula Mendes: One more nuance: Dedicated customers *do* expect more deterministic perf. Maybe numeric deltas are more acceptable there?

Dylan Brooks: Maybe in v2. For v1 we keep one policy across modes to avoid branching templates.

Marissa Cole: Agree. Keep v1 simple. Dedicated/Private customers can get deeper perf docs via their account team if needed.

Dev Patel: Works. Please just make sure the customer-facing note always includes “How to pin/rollback” link. That’s what people need during incidents.

Marissa Cole: Good call. Adding “Pinning + rollback docs” to required links.

Tessa Morgan: I’ll incorporate the “Performance section collapsed” + “Learn more links” behavior into the Console mocks.

Marissa Cole: Done. Thanks all.
